summary: Reports the work of an IAB advisory committee formed in 2003 to review how the IETF is administered, including its relationships with the RFC Editor, the IETF Secretariat and IANA, and to propose improvements. It did not look at the standards process itself. It is now marked historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The group that runs the internet's rule-making had paperwork and helpers to organize. A small team studied how they were set up and suggested ways to run things better.

questions: what is the ietf administrative structure
how is the ietf secretariat organized
subtitle: How the IETF's leadership and supporting organizations work together.

tldr.problem: As the IETF grew, its administrative structure became fragmented across multiple organizations with unclear relationships, funding pressures from declining meeting attendance, and gaps in institutional knowledge.
tldr.mechanism: An IAB Advisory Committee reviewed the IETF's relationships with the RFC Editor, IETF Secretariat, and IANA, documented problems, and proposed creating a formalized IETF organizational entity to manage resources and relationships directly.
tldr.outcome: This informational RFC is now historic and served as input to the creation of the IETF Administration LLC in 2006. The document's recommendations influenced how IETF administration was restructured.

today: RFC 3716 is now Historic. The recommendations led to the creation of the IETF Administration LLC in 2006, which formalized IETF administration as the RFC suggested. However, the RFC's specific organizational models were not adopted exactly as proposed, and the IETF's administrative structure has continued to evolve.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3716 documents the work of the IAB Advisory Committee, a group formed in fall 2003 to review the IETF's administrative structure. The committee examined how the IETF works with three key supporting organizations: the RFC Editor (at USC/ISI), the IETF Secretariat (at Foretec/CNRI), and the IANA (managed by ICANN).

The committee did not review the standards process itself; instead, it focused on the business of running the organization—budgets, staff, contracts, and decision-making processes. The RFC presents the committee's findings, the problems they identified, requirements for future success, and three possible organizational structures the IETF might adopt.
sections.plainLanguage: In 2003, the IETF leadership asked a group to study how the organization was run and suggest improvements. This document shows what they found.

sections.title: The IETF's Administrative Structure
sections.content:
The RFC maps out the functions and organizations involved in running the IETF. The IETF itself does not directly provide most of its own services; instead, several organizations volunteer or are contracted to provide support.

The IETF Secretariat at Foretec/CNRI handles day-to-day operations: managing working groups, coordinating meetings, running mailing lists, maintaining document repositories, and supporting the IESG and IAB telechats. The RFC Editor at USC/ISI, supported by ISOC, publishes the RFC document series and maintains the official standards status record. IANA, operated by ICANN under a memorandum of understanding, assigns protocol parameter numbers and maintains the registries. ISOC provides legal support, insurance, and funding for some RFC Editor costs.

The committee identified these supporting organizations and the informal relationships connecting them, noting that responsibility was distributed and often unclear.
sections.plainLanguage: Different organizations do different jobs: one runs the meetings, one publishes the documents, one keeps track of protocol numbers, and one pays the bills. But sometimes nobody knew exactly who was responsible for what.

sections.title: The Stress Points
sections.content:
The committee identified significant problems in the current structure. Financial stress was the most obvious: IETF meeting attendance had declined, reducing revenue from meeting fees. Budgetary deficits began in 2002 and were forecast to continue, draining the organization's reserves.

Beyond finance, the committee found several other problems. Responsibility for management and oversight was vague and scattered across organizations, making it unclear who could decide what. Institutional memory existed only in people's minds, creating risk during leadership transitions. Automation was lacking; routine administrative tasks required excessive manual work, slowing down simple requests. Relationships with supporting organizations were informal, sometimes documented only in vague understandings, which left supporting organizations uncertain about whom to take direction from and gave the IETF limited control over its services.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF had three big problems: it was running out of money because fewer people were attending meetings; nobody could agree on who was in charge of what; and the helpers doing the actual work did not know exactly what the IETF wanted from them.

sections.title: Requirements for Future Success
sections.content:
The committee then defined what the IETF would need to function better. Under Resource Management, the IETF needed budgetary autonomy to make hard choices about spending, a unified budget covering all funding sources, clear written contracts with supporting organizations, and the ability to develop new services as needed.

Stewardship required that the administration remain accountable to the IETF community, that responsibility and decision-making authority be clear to everyone, and that the IETF maintain persistent, accessible archives of its records so that future work could rely on documented history rather than oral tradition.

Working environment needed improvement through automation of mechanical tasks (so humans could focus on decisions requiring judgment) and better tools for standards development work.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF needed to control its own money, have clear written agreements with helpers, keep good records, and spend less time on paperwork.

sections.title: Proposed Organizational Structures
sections.content:
The committee proposed that the IETF become a formal organizational entity rather than an informal collection of relationships. This entity would directly manage finances, sign contracts, and be accountable to the IETF community.

The RFC outlined three possible structures. First, the IETF could be a dedicated activity within ISOC, using ISOC's existing legal standing and infrastructure but with dedicated IETF staff. Second, an ISOC subsidiary could be created—a separate legal entity focused solely on the IETF's mission, with its own governance structure but still connected to ISOC. Third, a completely independent IETF organization (called IETF Inc. or IETF LLC) could be formed, though the committee noted this carried financial and political risks during a period of organizational change.

The committee acknowledged that creating a formal structure would not immediately solve the IETF's financial problems, but believed it would provide the basis from which the right decisions could be made and acted upon.
sections.plainLanguage: The group suggested making the IETF an official organization that could sign contracts and control money, either as part of ISOC, as a separate company owned by ISOC, or as a completely independent company.
